paper.title: Naïve newsvendor adjustments: are they always detrimental?
paper.summary: Managers who order perishable stock often adjust the order that the textbook newsvendor formula suggests, either towards last period's demand (demand chasing) or towards average demand (pull-to-centre). Earlier studies treat both habits as mistakes. This paper asks whether they can help when the textbook order rests on an imperfect demand forecast. In simulations with 500 demand series, when a forecasting model of the right form was fitted to little data, modest adjustment reduced the profit loss of the textbook order by up to 5.1% over the first 90 periods. The gain shrank as data accumulated and turned into a loss on longer histories, and heavy demand chasing lost profit throughout. Profit was more sensitive to the amount of demand chasing than to the amount of pull-to-centre. When the forecasting model left out part of the demand process, or assumed normal noise when the noise was heavier-tailed, adjustment improved profit even with long histories, and pull-to-centre was the more useful of the two. A simple method that chooses the two adjustment weights by maximising past profit was tested on four products of a grocery store: it improved out-of-sample profit for every product, with each of five forecasting methods. The results come from one simulated demand process and one small real data set, and the gains under misspecification were judged from plots without statistical tests.

definitions.definition:
Single-product, single-period stochastic inventory problem. The demand $\tilde{d}$ over the selling period is a random variable with cumulative distribution function $F$. The product is bought before the period at unit price $v$ and sold during it at unit price $p$; each unit left over at the end of the period incurs a holding cost $c_h$, and each unit of unsatisfied demand a shortage cost $c_s$. For an order quantity $x$ and realised demand $d$, the realised profit is

$$\pi(x, d) = \begin{cases} p d - v x - c_h (x - d), & \text{if } x \geq d \\ p x - v x - c_s (d - x), & \text{if } x < d. \end{cases}$$

The order quantity that maximises expected profit is $x^* = F^{-1}(\tau)$, with overage cost $c_o = v + c_h$, underage cost $c_u = p - v + c_s$ and critical quantile $\tau = \frac{c_u}{c_o + c_u}$. A product with $\tau > 0.5$ is called high-margin, one with $\tau < 0.5$ low-margin.
The quantile $\tau = \frac{c_u}{c_o + c_u}$ of the demand distribution at which the [[D1:newsvendor problem]] is solved; also the target service level.

The order quantity for period $t$ obtained from the formula $x^*_t = F^{-1}(\tau)$ of the [[D1:newsvendor problem]], with the demand distribution's mean and standard deviation replaced by their estimates $\hat{\mu}_t$ and $\hat{\sigma}_t$ from a forecasting model fitted to the demands $d_1, \dots, d_{t-1}$.
The weight on the previous period's forecast error $d_{t-1} - x_{t-1}$ in the two-stage adjustment model; a higher value means stronger demand chasing.
The weight on the estimated mean demand in the two-stage adjustment model; a higher value means stronger pull-to-centre.

Adjustment of the order quantity towards the realised demand of the previous period. In its simplest model, taken from [[B2:Bostian et al. (2008)]],

$$x_t = x_{t-1} + \beta (d_{t-1} - x_{t-1}),$$

where $x_t$ is the order quantity in period $t$, $d_{t-1}$ the realised demand in the previous period and $\beta > 0$ the [[D7:demand chasing parameter]]. The model is simple exponential smoothing in error-correction form: it ignores the newsvendor solution and converges to the mean demand.

Adjustment of the order quantity towards the mean demand, also called the mean anchor heuristic:

$$x_t = (1 - \gamma) x^*_t + \gamma \hat{\mu}_t,$$

where $x^*_t$ is the [[D3:textbook order quantity]], $\hat{\mu}_t$ the estimated mean demand for period $t$ and $0 < \gamma < 1$ the [[D8:pull-to-centre parameter]].

Model of naïve adjustment in which [[D4:demand chasing]] is applied after [[D5:pull-to-centre]]:

$$\begin{aligned} x'_t &= (1 - \gamma) x^*_t + \gamma \hat{\mu}_t \\ x_t &= x'_t + \beta (d_{t-1} - x_{t-1}), \end{aligned}$$

which combine into the single formula

$$x_t = (1 - \gamma) x^*_t + \gamma \hat{\mu}_t + \beta (d_{t-1} - x_{t-1}).$$

Here $x^*_t$ is the [[D3:textbook order quantity]], $\hat{\mu}_t$ the estimated mean demand, $d_{t-1}$ the previous period's demand, $x_{t-1}$ the previous period's order, $\gamma$ the [[D8:pull-to-centre parameter]] and $\beta$ the [[D7:demand chasing parameter]]. The estimates $\hat{\mu}_t$, $x^*_t$ and $x_{t-1}$ all rest on $d_1, \dots, d_{t-1}$ and carry estimation error.

Profit shortfall of an order quantity $x_t$ against ordering the realised demand, in per cent:

$$\mathrm{PPL}(x_t) = 100 \, \frac{\pi(d_t, d_t) - \pi(x_t, d_t)}{\pi(d_t, d_t)},$$

with $\pi$ the profit of the [[D1:newsvendor problem]].

Improvement of the adjusted order quantity $x_t$ over the [[D3:textbook order quantity]] $x^*_t$ in [[D9:percentage profit loss]]:

$$\mathrm{RPI}(x_t) = 1 - \frac{\mathrm{PPL}(x_t)}{\mathrm{PPL}(x^*_t)}.$$

A positive value means the adjustment improved on the textbook order quantity; a negative value means it did worse. Also known as forecast value added.

500 simulated demand series of 200 periods each, generated with the `arima.sim()` function of the stats R package from an ARIMA(1,0,1) process with initial mean 10000 and normally distributed noise with standard deviation 100.
An ARIMA(1,0,1) forecasting model, the same form as the process generating the [[D11:simulated ARIMA(1,0,1) demand]], with its parameters estimated by maximum likelihood.
An MA(1) forecasting model fitted to the [[D11:simulated ARIMA(1,0,1) demand]]: it omits the autoregressive term of the generating process.
An ARIMA(2,0,1) forecasting model fitted to the [[D11:simulated ARIMA(1,0,1) demand]]: it has one redundant autoregressive term.

Demand series generated as the [[D11:simulated ARIMA(1,0,1) demand]] but with Laplace-distributed instead of normally distributed noise; the [[D3:textbook order quantity]] is computed under the incorrect assumption of normal noise.

For each series and a chosen forecasting model and pair $(\beta, \gamma)$: (a) for $t = 21, \dots, 200$, maximum-likelihood estimates $\hat{\mu}_t$ and $\hat{\sigma}_t$ of the mean and standard deviation of demand in period $t$ are obtained with the `arima()` function of the stats R package; (b) the [[D3:textbook order quantity]] $x^*_t$ is computed from $\tau$, $\hat{\mu}_t$ and $\hat{\sigma}_t$; (c) the order is set to $x_{20} = d_{20}$ and, for $t = 21, \dots, 200$, follows the [[D6:two-stage adjustment model]]. [[D10:Relative profit improvement]] is computed per period and averaged over the 500 series. The first 20 periods serve only for estimation, as estimates from fewer observations may be biased.

Choice of the parameters $\beta$ and $\gamma$ of the [[D6:two-stage adjustment model]] by maximising the in-sample empirical profit over a training set of periods $t \in [1, s]$, rather than by minimising the mean squared or mean absolute error:

$$\max_{\beta, \gamma} \sum_{t=2}^{s} \pi(x^*_t, \hat{\mu}_t, x_t, d_t),$$

where $x_t$ is computed from the forecasting model's $\hat{\mu}_t$, the [[D3:textbook order quantity]] $x^*_t$ and the realised demands. The maximisation uses a derivative-free algorithm, such as Nelder-Mead.

Daily demands of four perishable products, named A, B, C and D for confidentiality, from a medium-sized grocery store, over about 9 weeks from mid-October to December. The products were chosen to differ in data structure, prices, demands and critical quantiles; their prices and costs are given in the table.

tables.description: Selling price $p$, purchase price $v$, holding cost $c_h$, shortage cost $c_s$ and critical quantile $\tau$ of each product.

definitions.definition: Rolling origin with constant in-sample size: at each iteration three-fifths of a product's data form the training set, on which the [[D17:tuning heuristic]] is run, and a one-step-ahead forecast and order are made.
The `ets()` function of the forecast R package, which selects an ETS model by the Akaike Information Criterion; its forecasts give the [[D3:textbook order quantity]] before tuning.
The share of periods in which the order quantity covered the realised demand, compared with the target [[D2:critical quantile]].

claims.name: Modest adjustment raises profit on short data
claims.summary: When the right kind of demand model is used but fitted to little data, adding moderate demand chasing and pull-to-centre to the textbook order raises average profit, by up to 5.1% of the textbook order's profit loss.
claims.statement: With the [[D12:correctly specified ARIMA(1,0,1) model]] on the [[D11:simulated ARIMA(1,0,1) demand]] and $\tau = 0.7$, over the evaluation period $t \in [21, 110]$, the [[D6:two-stage adjustment model]] has a positive mean [[D10:relative profit improvement]] over the [[D3:textbook order quantity]] for every pair with $\beta \leq 0.3$ and $\gamma \leq 0.5$, the highest being 5.1% at $\beta = 0.2$ and $\gamma = 0.1$.

claims.summary: With little data, heavy demand chasing (a weight of 0.4 or more on last period's error) lowers profit compared with the textbook order, whatever the amount of pull-to-centre.
claims.statement: With the [[D12:correctly specified ARIMA(1,0,1) model]] on the [[D11:simulated ARIMA(1,0,1) demand]] and $\tau = 0.7$, over the evaluation period $t \in [21, 110]$, the [[D6:two-stage adjustment model]] has a negative mean [[D10:relative profit improvement]] over the [[D3:textbook order quantity]] for every pair with $\beta \geq 0.4$ and $\gamma \leq 0.5$.

claims.name: The benefit of adjustment fades as data accumulate
claims.summary: The profit gain from adjusting the textbook order is largest when few observations are available, shrinks as the history grows, and eventually turns into a loss.
claims.statement: With the [[D12:correctly specified ARIMA(1,0,1) model]] on the [[D11:simulated ARIMA(1,0,1) demand]] and $\tau = 0.7$, for each of the pairs $(\beta, \gamma) = (0, 0.4)$, $(0.1, 0)$ and $(0.2, 0.1)$, the mean [[D10:relative profit improvement]] of the [[D6:two-stage adjustment model]] over the [[D3:textbook order quantity]] is well above zero when the data are short, decreases as the data length grows, and eventually becomes negative.

claims.name: Small-sample estimation error explains the short-data gain
claims.summary: A likely reason for the gain on short data is that the estimated mean and spread of demand are error-prone, possibly biased, when few observations exist, and a small adjustment moves the order towards the true optimum.
claims.statement: The positive [[D10:relative profit improvement]] of modest adjustment on short simulated data may arise because maximum-likelihood estimates of the mean $\hat{\mu}_t$ and standard deviation $\hat{\sigma}_t$ of demand are prone to error, possibly with a systematic bias that decreases over time, when few observations are available, so that a small adjustment shifts the order quantity towards the true optimal value.

about.subject: small-sample estimation error of the mean and standard deviation of demand
about.relation: may explain
about.object: positive relative profit improvement of modest adjustment on short data

assessments.rationale: A tentative explanation the paper offers; it does not test the estimation bias directly.

Out-of-sample [[D10:relative profit improvement]] over the iterations is shown as boxplots per product (Figure 7 of the paper), the [[D21:achieved service level]] is compared with the target (table T1), and the experiment is repeated with four other forecasting methods (Mean, S-Mean, S-Naïve and ARIMA) in place of ETS (table T2).

warrants.text: Maximum-likelihood estimates of the mean and standard deviation of demand are prone to error on few observations, possibly with a bias that decreases as data accumulate. A small adjustment can then move the order quantity towards the true optimum, and this effect should vanish as more data become available, which is the pattern C4 reports.

A model that omits a variable attributes the omitted variation to noise and so over-estimates the demand variance, placing the newsvendor order further from the mean than required for $\tau \neq 0.5$. Pull-to-centre brings the order back towards the mean and so offsets this bias, consistent with the larger profit-maximising pull-to-centre parameter in C12.

limitations.statement: The simulations use a single generating process, an ARIMA(1,0,1) process with initial mean 10000 and noise standard deviation 100, so results for other demand processes are not shown.
The gains under misspecification are judged from boxplots and heat maps without a statistical test, and the paper reports no numerical values for them.
The real-life application covers four products of one grocery store over about 9 weeks of daily demand.
The parameter pair giving the highest relative profit improvement at $t = 21$ is read from a heat map and given only approximately.

open_questions.question: Whether the effect of naïve adjustment on profit is symmetric around $\tau = 0.5$ is suggested by similar results at $\tau = 0.3$ and $\tau = 0.7$ but not established.
Which other scenarios make naïve demand chasing or pull-to-centre adjustment beneficial is not characterised.
Whether forms of judgemental adjustment other than demand chasing and pull-to-centre improve newsvendor profit under scarce data or misspecification is not examined.
Whether behavioural experiments, in the laboratory or the field, confirm the simulated benefits of naïve adjustment is not established.
Whether the findings extend to multi-item newsvendor problems, with or without substitution between products, is not established.
